summary: This unit teaches you to run the front desk of a salon or spa: prepare the reception area, greet every person who comes in, find out why they have come and direct them to the right person or place. You will also learn to look after waiting clients and their belongings, use the telephone and take messages, deal with complaints, keep client information private, and keep the reception area safe and secure.

blocks.p: Reception is where a client forms her first opinion of a salon or spa, and where she forms her last one as she leaves. In this unit you learn the work of the person at the front desk: getting the area ready, welcoming clients and other visitors, finding out what each one needs, and sending or taking them to the right person. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. Even if you never work as a full-time receptionist, every stylist, nail technician and therapist takes a turn at the desk and answers the phone.

The unit is about people more than equipment. A receptionist needs a **neat appearance**, a **clear, friendly voice**, **good judgement** about who may go where, and the **discretion** to keep what she sees and hears to herself.

What this means at the desk

Clean, tidy and free of hazards before the first client
Phone, computer, till and appointment list ready
Present yourself professionally
Clean uniform, name badge, tidy hair, good personal hygiene
Polite, calm and attentive at all times
Greet clients and visitors
Notice everyone within moments of their coming in
Use a proper greeting and the client's name
Find the reason for each visit
Booked client, walk-in, new client, enquiry, delivery, sales representative, other visitor
Check the appointment book or system
Direct clients to the right person or area
Tell the stylist or therapist the client has arrived
Walk with her and introduce her; show changing rooms and facilities
Look after waiting clients and belongings
Explain delays honestly; offer a seat and a drink
Store belongings safely; valuables stay with the client
Use the telephone and take messages
Answer promptly with the standard greeting
Write complete messages, read them back and pass them on
Help clients with special needs
Ask how each client would like to be helped
Adapt how you speak, guide and seat people
Handle complaints and difficult moments
Listen, apologise, and pass on what you cannot solve
Protect privacy, security and safety

blocks.h: One arrival, from the door to the chair

flow: Find the reason for the visit
Check the booking; mark her arrived
Record form if she is new
Walk her through and introduce her

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks done as a group at the Centre's reception. You set up the desk and waiting area, then take turns as receptionist in role plays: clients on time and late, walk-ins, new clients, a wheelchair user, a sales representative and a stranger. You also answer practice phone calls, take messages, and help to make a reception guide poster for new staff.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Booking appointments and checking clients out (bills, payment, rebooking) belong to another unit. This unit stops when the client has been handed over to the person who will serve her.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A client decides within seconds whether a business is clean, organised and worth her money. She makes that decision at reception, from two things: what the area looks like, and what you look like.

flow: Check for hazards; clear the exits
Clean and tidy the desk and waiting area
Switch on and test the phone, computer and till
Set out water, magazines and the price list

head: Check
What 'ready' looks like
rows: Desk
Wiped and clear. Pens, message pad, appointment cards and the appointment book or screen ready. No food, drinks, handbags or personal phones on show.
Waiting area
Seats wiped, floor swept and dry, bins emptied, magazines current and neatly stacked, price list and service menu out, water and cups ready.
Entrance, glass and retail display
Door and windows clean; display shelves dusted, stocked and priced.
Equipment
Phone, computer or tablet, card machine and till switched on and working. Report anything that is not.
Messages
Voicemail and overnight messages listened to, written down and passed on. A message asking to cancel or change a booking is dealt with first.
The day's appointments
You know who is coming, when, for what and with whom. Early bookings, new clients, large groups and special needs are pointed out to the staff.
Hazards
No bags, boxes or cables in walkways; mats flat; fire exit and its path clear; lights working.
Atmosphere
Comfortable temperature, good light, soft music at a level people can talk over. Follow the salon's own standard.

blocks.p: Keep it that way all day. Clear used cups, straighten the magazines, wipe the desk and sweep up tracked-in hair whenever you have a quiet moment.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Wear a clean, pressed uniform and your **name badge**
Keep your hair neat and your nails clean
Wear light make-up and little jewellery, as the salon's dress code allows
Stand or sit upright, facing the door
Wear yesterday's uniform, or strong perfume
Chew gum or eat at the desk: it looks unprofessional and makes your speech unclear
Use your own phone, or chat with co-workers, in front of clients
Slouch, yawn or lean on the desk

blocks.p: **Personal hygiene** means taking care of your own body: a daily bath or shower, deodorant, clean teeth and fresh breath, clean hands and nails, and clean clothes. You work close to people, in a business that sells grooming. A receptionist who looks and smells fresh tells clients that the whole salon keeps high standards.

blocks.note: The receptionist is part of what the business is selling. If your own hair, nails and skin are well kept, clients trust the salon's services before they have tried them.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Greeting people and finding out why they have come

ul: Greet every person **as soon as they come in**, or within a few moments. A person left standing unnoticed feels unwelcome, however good the service is later.
Look up, make eye contact and smile before you speak.

Use a standard greeting with three parts: the **time of day**, a **welcome with the name of the business**, and an **offer of help**. For example: 'Good afternoon, welcome to the salon. How may I help you?'
Use the client's title and name once you know it: 'Miss Thompson', 'Mr. Brown'. People feel recognised and valued when they hear their own name. Use a first name only if the client invites you to.

If you are busy, on the phone or with another client, show the newcomer you have seen her: look up, smile, nod or raise a hand, and help her as soon as you are free. Do not ignore her until you have finished, and do not cut off the caller without a word.

blocks.note: Avoid greetings that sound careless or unwelcoming: 'Yes?', 'What do you want?', 'Hold on.' Friendly does not mean over-familiar: 'Hi darling' is not a professional greeting for a client you do not know.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Who has come in, and what do they need?

blocks.p: Never assume. A polite, open question, 'How may I help you today?', tells you the **reason for the visit**, and the reason tells you what to do next and where the person should go.

head: Who
What you do
rows: A client with an appointment
Ask her name and **check the appointment book or system** first: name, time, service and staff member
Mark her as arrived and tell the stylist or therapist
If the booking is not there, stay calm: check the spelling, other days and other staff, then offer the nearest suitable time. Do not argue about whose mistake it was
A new client
Welcome her warmly and ask her to fill in a **client record or consultation form**
Explain why: so the staff can serve her safely and contact her about bookings
Show her where things are: waiting area, washroom, changing room
A walk-in (no appointment)
Find out the service she wants
Check the book for a staff member who is **trained for that service and free for long enough**
If there is a slot, offer it and book her in
If not, apologise and offer the next free time or another day; take her name and number
A regular client whose details may have changed
Check that the phone number on her record is still correct, quietly, so that the salon can reach her about bookings.
Someone with an enquiry
Answer from the price list or service menu. If you do not know, find out from a stylist or the supervisor; do not guess at prices, times or what a service can achieve.
A client for a chemical service
Look at her record. If a skin test is needed and none is recorded, **tell the stylist or therapist before the service starts**. The decision is theirs, not yours.

blocks.p: Work out how late she is and how much of her time is left. A client booked for 10:15 a.m. who arrives at 10:40 a.m. is 25 minutes late. If she was booked for a 60-minute service and the staff member has another client straight after, only 35 minutes are left.

ul: Greet her as warmly as any other client. Do not scold.
Check with the staff member what can be done in the time that is left.
Explain politely and offer a choice: a **shorter or changed service** now, **waiting** for the next free time, or a **new appointment**.
The client who comes after her must not be made to wait because of someone else's lateness.

blocks.p: Ask the supervisor. A receptionist is expected to know the salon's services, prices, opening hours, staff and their skills, and its policies. Nobody expects a trainee to know everything on the first day, but everyone expects her to ask instead of guessing.

Not everyone who comes to the desk wants a service. Each visitor is greeted with the same courtesy as a client, and each is asked how you can help. What differs is **where they are allowed to go**. Work areas and treatment rooms are for staff and the clients being served. Stock rooms, the office and the till are for staff only.

head: Visitor
What you do
What you do not do
rows: Sales representative (a person who visits to sell a supplier's products)
Take his **name and company**; ask for a business card
Ask him to take a seat
Check whether the owner or manager is free to see him, or wants him to make an appointment
Send him through to the back, give out the owner's personal number, or place an order yourself.
Delivery
Check the delivery is addressed to your salon
Call the person who receives stock, so that the goods can be **checked against the delivery note** before anything is signed
Have boxes put where they block nobody, and moved to the stock room promptly
Sign for goods nobody has checked, leave boxes in a walkway or by the fire exit, or let the driver wander through the salon.
Someone to see a member of staff (family, a friend)
Take the name and tell the staff member
Ask the visitor to wait in reception
Interrupt a service for anything but an emergency, or send the visitor to the work area.
A job seeker
Accept the application or take the details, and say who will be in touch, as the salon's practice allows.
Promise an interview or discuss wages.
An official visitor (for example a public health or fire inspector)
Greet him politely and ask to see identification
Tell the owner or manager at once
Leave him unattended, or try to answer his questions about the business yourself.
A person who will not say why he is there, or who walks past the desk
Step forward, greet him and ask politely: 'Good morning, sir. May I help you? Who are you here to see?'
If you are uneasy, call the supervisor
Ignore him, shout across the salon, or leave the desk to chase him through the treatment rooms.

blocks.note: Challenging a stranger politely is good service and good security at once. A real visitor is glad to be helped. A person with no business in the building learns that he has been noticed.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Looking after a client who is waiting

blocks.p: Waiting is the part of a visit that clients like least, and most complaints about waiting are really complaints about **not being told**. A client who is kept informed and comfortable will usually wait calmly.

flow: Tell her about the delay at once
Tell the staff member she is waiting
Check on her every few minutes

ul: Tell her as soon as she arrives, not after she has sat wondering for a quarter of an hour.
Be honest. If the stylist will be 20 minutes, say 20 minutes. 'She will soon come' means nothing, and a wait that turns out longer than promised makes people angrier than the truth would have.
Offer **choices**: wait, come back a little later, see another staff member who is free and has the skills (only if she is happy with that), or rebook.
Offer a comfortable seat, water or a drink, and something to read, such as magazines, the service menu or the price list.
Go back to her with updates. Do not let her feel forgotten.

blocks.p: A client's **belongings** are her own things: handbag, phone, coat, umbrella, shopping, jewellery.

ul: Offer to take umbrellas, coats and bulky bags, and put them in the salon's usual place: a coat stand, a cupboard or lockers. If the salon uses tickets or labels, use them, so that every item goes back to its owner.
**Valuables stay with the client**, or go in a secure, lockable place if the salon provides one. That way they are not lost, damaged or stolen during the service, and the salon is not blamed.
Do not put belongings on the floor behind the desk, where they are in the way, or anywhere a passer-by could reach them.
When she leaves, return her things and check she has everything.

blocks.p: Pointing and saying 'She's over there' is not directing. A salon is a confusing place on a first visit, and a spa even more so.

ul: Tell the stylist or therapist that the client has arrived, and wait until she is ready.
**Walk with** the client at her pace, a little ahead and to one side, warning her of steps, wet floors or trailing cables.
**Introduce** her by name, and say what she is booked for: 'Miss Thompson, this is Andrea, who will be doing your facial today. Andrea, Miss Thompson is here for her 2 o'clock deep-cleansing facial.'

For a service that needs her to change (a body treatment, a massage, waxing), show a first-time client the **changing room**, the **gown or robe** and how to wear it, the **locker or place for her things**, and the washroom. Tell her where to go, or who will come for her, when she has changed.
Do not leave the desk unattended for long while you do this. If the walk is long, ask a co-worker to cover or to take the client through.

blocks.note: In a hotel spa, many guests are visitors to Jamaica. Prices may be quoted in J$ and US$, and guests may ask about more than the spa. Keep to what you know, and send other questions to the hotel's front desk or guest services.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: You communicate in two ways at once. **Spoken (verbal)** communication is your words and your voice. **Unspoken (non-verbal)** communication, or body language, is everything else: your face, eyes, posture and gestures. When the two disagree, people believe the body.

head: Channel
Welcoming
Unwelcoming
rows: Spoken
A warm greeting, using the client's name
A clear voice at an even pace
Plain, polite words: 'please', 'thank you', 'certainly'
Standard English with clients, whatever is spoken among friends
Mumbling, or speaking too fast
Slang, or salon jargon the client does not know
Sighing; a bored or sharp tone
Talking over the client
Unspoken
Eye contact and a smile
An open posture: facing the person, arms relaxed
Nodding as she speaks
Standing up to greet her
Looking at a phone or a screen while she talks
Folded arms; turning away
Rolling the eyes; watching the clock
Carrying on a conversation with a co-worker

ul: Give the speaker your whole attention and let her finish.
Use **open questions**, which often start with 'how', 'what' or 'why' and let the client answer in her own words, to find out what she needs: 'What would you like done today?'
Use closed questions to confirm facts: 'Is that with Marcia, at two o'clock?'

If you did not catch something, say so politely and ask her to repeat it: 'I'm sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you say it again for me?' Then **repeat it back** to check. Guessing leads to wrong bookings and wrong messages.
Write down names, numbers, dates and times as you hear them.

blocks.p: Treat every client with the same respect, speak **to the client herself** and not only to the person with her, and **ask what help she would like** before you give any. People know their own needs better than you can guess them.

head: Client
How you help
rows: Uses a wheelchair
Greet her as you would anyone else, at eye level if the talk is long
Ask how she would like to be helped; do not push the chair or touch it without asking
Clear the path: move chairs, mats, boxes and trolleys; hold doors
Check with staff that the treatment area can be reached; many services can be done with the client in her own chair
Is hard of hearing
Face her, in good light, so that she can see your lips and face
Speak clearly, at a normal pace, without shouting
Cut down background noise if you can
Write down times, prices and instructions
Is blind or has poor sight
Say who you are and that you are speaking to her
Offer your arm, and let her take it; describe steps and turns
Read out forms and the price list, and help her complete them privately
Is elderly, or walks slowly
Walk at her pace; offer an arm if she wishes
Offer a seat near the desk and near the door of the treatment area
Give her time; do not hurry her words or her steps
Speaks little English
Speak slowly and clearly in short, simple sentences; do not raise your voice
Use gestures, pictures, the price list and the service menu
Write down the time and the price
Ask a colleague who speaks her language, if there is one
Has brought a young child
Welcome the child too
Ask politely that the child stays with the parent or another adult, in the waiting area, **away from work areas**, where hot tools, chemicals, sharp tools and wet floors could hurt him
A receptionist is not a childminder and cannot be responsible for the child

blocks.note: Patience is the most useful tool you have. No client should be made to feel that she is a nuisance because she needs a little more time or a different kind of help.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: To a caller, you **are** the salon. She cannot see your smile, the clean desk or your uniform; she has only your voice. Many clients phone before they ever visit, so the call may be the first impression.

flow: Greeting + business name + your name + offer of help
Deal with the call, or take a message
Let the caller hang up first

ul: Answer **promptly**, within about three rings. A phone that rings on and on tells the caller nobody cares.
Smile as you pick up: a smile can be heard in the voice. Put down anything you are eating or drinking first.

Use the salon's standard greeting. It has four parts: the time of day, the **name of the business**, **your own name**, and an offer of help. For example: 'Good morning, Coral Bay Salon, Shanice speaking. How may I help you?'
Speak clearly and a little more slowly than face to face. Keep background noise and side conversations away from the phone.

A client standing in front of you and a ringing phone both need attention. Excuse yourself to the client, answer the call, and either deal with it quickly or ask the caller whether she can hold or be called back.
**Ask first**: 'May I put you on hold for a moment while I check?' Wait for the answer.
Use the **hold button**. Do not lay the handset on the desk or cover it with your hand: the caller hears everything said near it.
Come back within about half a minute. If you need longer, go back to the caller, say so, and offer to call her back.
Thank her for holding.

blocks.h: When the person asked for is busy

blocks.p: A stylist or therapist is never called away from a client to take an ordinary call. Say that she is with a client, and offer to **take a message** or to have her **call back**. Do not say where she is or what she is doing in more detail than that. If the caller only needs information you can give, such as a price or an opening time, give it.

head: Every message needs
Why
rows: Who the message is **for**
So that it reaches the right person.
The **caller's name** (and company, if any)
So that the right person is called back. Ask for the spelling if you are unsure.
The caller's **phone number**
Even if 'she has it'. Numbers change, and it saves time.
The **message** itself, and what the caller wants done
'Please call back', 'will call again', 'wishes to cancel Friday's appointment'.
The **date and time** of the call
So that the reader knows how old the message is and how urgent.
**Your name** or initials
So that the reader knows whom to ask about it.

ul: Write on the **message pad** kept by the phone, not on scraps of paper or your hand.
**Read the message back** to the caller, with the number said digit by digit, to check that every detail is right.
Tell the caller honestly when she can expect a reply.
**Pass the message on as soon as possible**: hand it to the person, or put it in the place the salon uses for messages, and mention it. A perfect message that stays on the pad is useless.
A message is private. Do not read it out across the salon.

blocks.p: On a poor line, letters such as B, D, P and T, or M and N, sound alike. The international phonetic alphabet gives each letter a word that cannot be mistaken.

head: A–G
H–N
O–U
V–Z
rows: Alfa
Hotel
Oscar
Victor
Bravo
India
Papa
Whiskey
Charlie
Juliett
Quebec
X-ray
Delta
Kilo
Romeo
Yankee
Echo
Lima
Sierra
Zulu
Foxtrot
Mike

(none)
Golf

Uniform
(none)

blocks.p: To check the surname 'Dacres', you would say: 'D for Delta, A for Alfa, C for Charlie, R for Romeo, E for Echo, S for Sierra.'

blocks.note: Never give a caller a client's phone number or address, or say whether a particular client is in the salon, whoever the caller says they are. Offer to pass a message to the client instead.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Sooner or later an unhappy client will come to the desk, because the desk is where clients come. A complaint handled well often keeps the client; a complaint handled badly loses her and everyone she tells.

flow: Move to a quieter spot if you can
Solve it if you are allowed; if not, fetch the supervisor
Tell her who will help her

head: Step
How
Why
rows: Stay calm and polite
Keep your voice low and even. The anger is about the problem, not about you.
A raised voice answered with a raised voice becomes a quarrel.
Take it somewhere quieter
'Mrs. Grant, would you come and sit over here with me so that I can give this my full attention?'
Gives her privacy and keeps other clients from being upset.
Listen to the whole complaint
Do not interrupt, correct or explain. Nod. Take notes.
She calms down as she is heard, and you need the facts.
Apologise
'I am sorry you are not happy with your nails.'
It is an apology for her experience. It does not say who was at fault, and you must not blame a co-worker.
Check your understanding
'So two nails lifted the day after your appointment. Is that right?'
Shows you listened and gives the supervisor accurate facts.
Pass it on
If the answer is outside your authority, tell her you are fetching the supervisor or manager, give that person's **name**, and fetch her straight away.
A receptionist does not decide on refunds, free services or re-dos. Promising them is not yours to do.
Record it
In the salon's complaint record: date, client, the complaint, what was done, by whom.
So that it is followed up and the salon can learn from it.

ul: Argue, contradict her or say 'That's not my job'.
Discuss the complaint in front of other clients, or gossip about it afterwards.
Blame the stylist, the client or the products.
Promise a refund, a discount or a free service that you have no authority to give.
Leave her standing at the desk with no idea what will happen next.

blocks.note: If a person becomes abusive or threatening, do not argue and do not try to handle it alone. Call the supervisor at once. If anyone is in danger, call the police on 119.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Confidentiality** means keeping clients' personal details private and not sharing them. The desk holds a great deal of private information: names, phone numbers and addresses, health conditions and allergies, the services people have and what they pay. Clients give it in trust. If it leaks, a client can be embarrassed, upset or even put at risk, and the business loses her trust and may break the law.

blocks.note: Jamaica's **Data Protection Act**, passed in 2020, requires businesses to keep people's personal information safe, to collect only what they need, and to use it only for the purpose it was given for. A salon's client records, on paper or on a computer, are covered by it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Situation
What you do
rows: Record cards and forms
Keep them in a closed file or locked drawer, not spread on the desk. Give a new client somewhere private to fill in her form.
The booking screen or appointment book
Turn the screen away from the waiting area; close the book. Lock the screen when you leave the desk.
Another client asks who is in today, or what someone is having done
Explain politely that you cannot share other clients' details.
A caller asks for a client's number or address, or whether she is in the salon
Do not give it, even to someone who says they are family. Offer to pass on a message to the client.
Talking about a client's details at the desk
Speak quietly, and only to those who need to know.
Outside work, and on social media
Say nothing about who comes to the salon or what they have done.

ul: **Do not leave the desk empty for long.** Clients arriving need help, the phone needs answering, and an empty desk leaves cash, records and clients' belongings unguarded.
If you must leave, ask a co-worker to cover. If nobody can, close the till, lock the screen and put record cards away first.
Keep the till closed between sales and the cash out of sight. Keep handbags and stored belongings out of reach of the public side of the desk.
Greet every person who comes in, and politely stop anyone you do not know from walking through to the work areas or treatment rooms.
Report anything suspicious to the supervisor.

head: Hazard
What you do
rows: A bag strap, box or cable lying across a walkway
Move it at once; it is a trip hazard. Ask clients kindly to keep bags under their seats.
A spill, or a floor wet from umbrellas on a rainy day
Put out a **wet floor sign** and wipe it up straight away. Leave the sign until the floor is dry.
A curled mat, a loose tile, a wobbly chair, a failed light
Take it out of use or mark it, and report it.
Boxes or furniture near the fire exit
Clear them. The exit and the way to it must be free at all times, so that everyone can get out quickly and safely.
Overloaded sockets and trailing extension cords at the desk
Report them; do not add more plugs.

flow: Stop work; raise the alarm if it has not sounded
Help clients and visitors out by the nearest safe exit
Take the day's appointment list if it is safe
Check everyone is out, using the list

ul: Treat every alarm as real. Do not stop to finish a phone call, collect belongings or count the till.
Give clear, calm instructions: clients, some of them in gowns with products on their hair, will look to you.
Help anyone who needs it: a client using a wheelchair, an older client, a child.
The **assembly point** is the safe place outside where everyone meets. The appointment list shows who was in the building, so that the person in charge can check that everyone is out.
Stay out until the person in charge, or the fire brigade, says it is safe.

head: Emergency
Number in Jamaica
rows: Police
Fire brigade
Ambulance

blocks.p: When you call, say **what** has happened, **where** you are (the name of the business, the street, the town and a landmark), and **how many** people are hurt. Stay on the line until you are told to hang up. Keep the numbers, and the salon's own address, written beside the phone.

ul: I can prepare the reception and waiting area before the first client and keep it tidy all day.
I can describe professional presentation and personal hygiene for a receptionist.
I can greet a person promptly with a proper greeting, even when I am busy or on the phone.
I can find the reason for a visit and check the appointment book or system.
I can deal with a booked client, a new client, a walk-in and a late client.
I can work out how late a client is and how much of her booked time is left.
I can deal correctly with a sales representative, a delivery, an official visitor and a stranger.
I can look after a waiting client and explain a delay honestly.
I can store belongings safely and explain why valuables stay with the client.
I can walk a client to her stylist or therapist and introduce her, and show a new client the changing room.
I can use welcoming spoken and unspoken communication, and repeat details back to check them.
I can help a client who uses a wheelchair, is hard of hearing, has poor sight, is elderly, speaks little English or has a child with her.
I can answer the phone with the standard greeting, put a caller on hold correctly and take a complete message.
I can spell a name with the phonetic alphabet.
I can receive a complaint calmly and pass it to the supervisor.
I can keep client information confidential, and name the law that protects it.
I can keep the desk, cash, records and belongings secure.
I can spot and deal with hazards at reception.
I can say what to do when the fire alarm sounds, and give the emergency numbers.

blocks.note: In essay answers, describe what you would do in order, and give the reason for the important steps. For example: 'I read the message back to the caller, so that I am sure the name and number are right.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Reception
The area at the front of the business where clients are greeted and booked in.
Waiting area
The part of the salon where clients sit before their service.
First impression
The opinion a client forms in the first few moments of her visit or call.
Name badge
The small sign on a uniform that tells clients the worker's name.
Personal presentation
How you look and carry yourself: uniform, hair, nails, posture.
Personal hygiene
Taking care of your own body: washing, clean teeth, fresh breath, clean clothes.
Appointment book / system
The paper book or computer system that shows who is booked, when, for what and with whom.
Walk-in
A client who comes in without an appointment.
Client record (consultation) form
The form a new client fills in with her contact details and information the staff need.
Sales representative
A person who visits to sell a supplier's products to the owner.
Delivery note
The supplier's list of the goods in a delivery, used to check them.
Belongings
A client's own things, such as her handbag, phone and coat.
Valuables
Belongings worth a lot or hard to replace: money, phone, jewellery.
Gown
The cover put on a client to protect her clothes during a hair or spa service.
Directing
Taking or sending a client to the right person or area.
Verbal communication
What you say and how you say it.
Non-verbal communication (body language)
Messages sent by the face, eyes, posture and gestures.
Open posture
Facing the person with arms relaxed, not folded.
Open question
A question, often starting with how, what or why, that lets the client answer in her own words.
Closed question
A question answered with 'yes', 'no' or one short fact.
Special needs
Extra or different help a client requires, for example because of a disability, age or language.
Hold
Keeping a caller waiting on the line, with her agreement, using the hold button.
Message pad
The pad or book kept by the phone for writing down calls.
Phonetic alphabet
A set of words (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie...) used to spell names clearly.
Complaint
A client's statement that she is not satisfied.
Complaint record
The book or file where complaints and what was done about them are written.
Confidentiality
Keeping clients' personal details private and not sharing them.
Data Protection Act
The Jamaican law, passed in 2020, that protects people's personal information.
Security
Protecting people, cash, records and property from theft and harm.
Hazard
Anything that could cause harm, such as a spill or a cable across a walkway.
Wet floor sign
A warning sign put out until a wet floor is dry.
Fire exit
A door kept clear for leaving the building in an emergency.
Assembly point
The safe place outside where everyone meets after leaving the building.
The number for the police in Jamaica.
The number for the fire brigade and ambulance in Jamaica.

c1.title: Opening time at a hotel spa in Negril
c1.text: Kemar Whyte is the receptionist at a hotel spa in Negril. He arrives at 8:30 a.m.; the first guest is booked for 9:00 a.m. Three boxes of massage oil, delivered late yesterday, are stacked in the corridor in front of the fire exit. The voicemail light on the phone is flashing. Yesterday's used cups are still on the waiting-area table. Kemar's uniform shirt is clean, but he has left his name badge at home.

c2.title: A busy Saturday in Old Harbour
c2.text: Shanique Barrett is at the desk of a hair and barber salon in Old Harbour. At 10:55 a.m. she is on the phone with a client who is asking about prices when two people come in together. Mrs. Verona Lewis has an 11:00 a.m. wash and set with the stylist Marva, who is running 25 minutes behind. Mr. Andre Francis has no appointment and wants a haircut; the only barber, Dwight, is booked solid until 1:30 p.m.

c3.title: Calls for Mrs. Chin
c3.text: At a salon in Mandeville, the owner, Mrs. Chin, has gone to the bank and will be back at about 2:00 p.m. At 12:10 p.m. trainee Latoya answers a call from a Mr. Fitzroy Dacres of a beauty supply company, who says Mrs. Chin's order will be two days late and asks her to call him. The line is poor. A few minutes later a woman phones, says she is the sister of a regular client, Miss Kerry Vassell, and asks for Kerry's new mobile number 'because I lost my phone'.

c4.title: Lifted nails in Ocho Rios
c4.text: On Monday morning Mrs. Sandra Pryce walks into a nail bar in Ocho Rios, where three clients are being served and two are waiting. She holds out her hand to the receptionist, Althea, and says loudly that the gel nails she paid J$6,500 for on Saturday have lifted already, that the technician was careless, and that she wants her money back now. The technician, Jody, is with a client. The supervisor, Miss Hall, is in the office.

c5.title: An unexpected visitor and an alarm in Linstead
c5.text: At a salon in Linstead, receptionist Trudy-Ann is alone at the desk at 3:00 p.m. A man she has never seen, in overalls and with no identification showing, walks in, says 'air conditioning' without stopping, and heads for the door to the treatment rooms. Twenty minutes later a hood dryer at the back starts to smoke and the fire alarm sounds. There are six clients in the salon, one of them an elderly lady who uses a walking frame. A client in a gown turns back to fetch her handbag from the cupboard.

questions.q: Kemar has half an hour before the first guest. Which job should he do first?
o: Have the boxes moved away from the fire exit to the stock room
Listen to the voicemail messages and write each one down
Clear the used cups and wipe down the waiting-area table
Print the day's appointment list for the therapists
questions.why: A blocked fire exit is a danger to everyone in the building and is put right before anything else. The messages, the cups and the list all matter, but none of them can hurt anybody.

questions.q: One voicemail is from a guest who cannot keep her 9:00 a.m. massage. What should Kemar do with it?
o: Write it on the message pad and hand it over at the lunch break
Act on it straight away: update the booking and tell the therapist
Leave it on the voicemail so that the manager can hear it herself
Wait until 9:15 a.m. to see whether the guest turns up after all
questions.why: Overnight messages are checked before opening because some change the day. A cancellation is dealt with at once, so the therapist is not left waiting and the time can be offered to someone else.

questions.q: Why does it matter that Kemar has no name badge today?
o: Guests cannot tell who he is or address him by name
A badge is needed to operate the till and the card machine
Without a badge he may not legally greet hotel guests
The badge is what shows guests that his uniform is clean
questions.why: The name badge tells clients the worker's name and that he belongs to the business, which helps them to trust him and to ask for him again. He should tell the supervisor and ask for a temporary one.

questions.q: Shanique is still on the phone when Mrs. Lewis and Mr. Francis reach the desk. What should she do at that moment?
o: Put the phone down on the desk and deal with the two of them first
Finish the call fully before she looks up, so the caller has her attention
Look up, smile and signal that she will be with them in a moment
Point Mrs. Lewis to Marva's station and hold up a hand to Mr. Francis
questions.why: People at the desk must know at once that they have been seen, but a caller is not dropped or left to overhear. A look, a smile and a small gesture do both; then she finishes the call politely and quickly.

questions.q: What is the best thing to say to Mrs. Lewis about her 11:00 a.m. appointment?
o: 'Marva will soon come, Mrs. Lewis. Have a seat over there and she will call you as soon as she is ready for you, all right?'
'Marva is about 25 minutes behind, I am sorry. Would you like to wait, with some water, or shall I find you another time?'
'You are a little early, so Marva is not ready. Please take a seat and I will let you know when it is 11 o'clock, Mrs. Lewis.'
'Marva is still on her last client, who came late. It is not her fault, so please be patient with us this morning, Mrs. Lewis.'
questions.why: Tell the client about the delay at once, give the honest length of the wait, apologise, make her comfortable and offer a choice. 'Soon come' tells her nothing, and blaming another client is unprofessional.

questions.q: What should Shanique offer Mr. Francis, the walk-in?
o: A haircut from Marva as soon as she has finished Mrs. Lewis
A seat in the waiting area in case one of Dwight's clients is late
A place ahead of Dwight's next client, as he is already in the salon
The 1:30 p.m. slot with Dwight, or a booking on another day
questions.why: A walk-in is offered the next free time with a staff member trained for the service. Booked clients are not pushed back for him, a stylist is not given work she is not trained for, and he is not left to wait with no promise.

questions.q: When Marva is ready, how should Shanique direct Mrs. Lewis?
o: Call across to Marva that her eleven o'clock is waiting for her
Walk with her to the station and introduce her to Marva by name
Tell Mrs. Lewis that Marva is at the third chair on the left
Ask the client waiting beside her to show her where Marva works
questions.why: Directing means taking the client to the right person and introducing her, with the service she is booked for. Shouting across the salon and pointing are careless and announce her business to everyone.

questions.q: Latoya is not sure she has Mr. Dacres's surname right on the poor line. What should she do?
o: Ask him to spell it, and check each letter back: 'D for Delta, A for Alfa...'
Write it the way it sounds, as Mrs. Chin will know who he is
Leave the surname off the message and write 'Fitzroy from the supplier'
Ask him to send the details in an e-mail instead of leaving a message
questions.why: A message is only useful if the name and number are right. Asking for the spelling and checking it with the phonetic alphabet removes the doubt; guessing or leaving it out passes the problem to Mrs. Chin.

questions.q: Which message for Mrs. Chin is complete?
o: For Mrs. Chin. Mr. F. Dacres, beauty supplier, 876-555-0142: order two days late, please call him. 12:10 p.m., 14 June. Latoya
For Mrs. Chin. A man from the supplier rang at lunch time about the order being late. He says you have his number. Latoya
Mr. Dacres rang, 876-555-0142, at 12:10 p.m. on 14 June. He will explain about the order when somebody calls him back.
For Mrs. Chin. Mr. Dacres called at 12:10 p.m., 14 June, about your order. I told him you are at the bank until 2:00. Latoya
questions.why: A complete message says who it is for, who called and from where, the number, the message and what is wanted, the date and time, and who took it. Each of the others leaves out the caller's name or number, the message, or who it is for.

questions.q: What should Latoya do about the woman who asks for Kerry Vassell's new number?
o: Give it, since the caller knows Kerry's name and that she is a regular
Decline politely, and offer to pass a message to Kerry
Give only the last four digits, so that the sister can check her own record
Ask her a question that only Kerry's sister could answer, then give it
questions.why: A client's contact details are never given out, even to someone who says she is family: the salon cannot check who is calling, and the information is Kerry's. Passing on a message lets Kerry decide for herself.

questions.q: Mrs. Chin comes back at 2:00 p.m. and goes straight into a meeting with a sales representative. What should Latoya do with the message about the late order?
o: Keep it on the pad until closing time, when Mrs. Chin checks the desk
Call Mr. Dacres herself and tell him the late delivery is acceptable
Hand it to her, or put it where she will see it, as soon as she is back
Read it out to her from the desk as she walks through with her visitor
questions.why: A message is passed on as soon as possible, quietly. A trainee does not answer a supplier on the owner's behalf, and business messages are not announced in front of visitors.

questions.q: What should Althea do first?
o: Tell her firmly that shouting will not get the problem solved
Stay calm and ask Mrs. Pryce to sit with her somewhere quieter
Call Jody away from her client to come and look at the nails
Explain that gel nails can lift if they are not cared for at home
questions.why: The first step is to stay calm and give the client privacy and attention. Scolding her, pulling the technician off another client or explaining why it may be her own fault all make an angry client angrier.

questions.q: Mrs. Pryce repeats that the technician was careless. Which reply is best?
o: 'I am sorry. Jody is quite new, and she does sometimes rush her gel work.'
'I am sorry you are unhappy with your nails. Let me check I have this right.'
'I am sorry, but nobody else has ever complained about Jody's gel work before.'
'I am sorry. That should not have happened; it was clearly our mistake.'
questions.why: Apologise that the client is unhappy and check the facts back. A receptionist does not blame a co-worker, contradict the client or admit fault on the salon's behalf: she does not yet know what went wrong.

questions.q: Mrs. Pryce demands her J$6,500 back at once. What should Althea do?
o: Refund the money from the till so that the other clients are not disturbed
Offer a free set of nails on another day in place of the refund
Say she will fetch Miss Hall, the supervisor, and do so immediately
Explain that the salon does not give refunds once a service is done
questions.why: Refunds, free services and re-dos are decided by the supervisor or manager, not at the desk. Althea tells the client who will help her, by name, and fetches that person straight away.

questions.q: After Miss Hall has dealt with Mrs. Pryce, what should be written in the complaint record?
o: The date, the client's name, what she complained of and what was done
Only the amount refunded, as the till has to balance at the end of the day
Althea's opinion of how the client behaved in front of other clients
Nothing, if the client left satisfied and no money was returned
questions.why: Every complaint is recorded with the date, the client, the complaint, the action taken and by whom, so that it can be followed up and the salon can learn from it.

questions.q: What should Trudy-Ann do as the man in overalls heads for the treatment rooms?
o: Let him go through, as a workman in overalls is clearly there to work
Follow him through the treatment rooms to see what he does there
Call the police on 119 before he reaches the treatment-room door
Step forward, greet him and ask who he is and whom he has come to see
questions.why: Nobody the receptionist does not know goes past the desk unchallenged. A polite question stops him, protects clients' privacy and property, and lets the supervisor confirm whether he is expected. Following him leaves the desk empty.

questions.q: The alarm is sounding. What is Trudy-Ann's main job now?
o: Calmly direct clients and visitors out by the nearest safe exit
Go to the back of the salon to find out whether the fire is real
Lock the till and put the record cards away before she leaves
Telephone each stylist's next client to say there will be a delay
questions.why: When the alarm sounds, people come first: everyone leaves by the nearest safe exit and goes to the assembly point. Every alarm is treated as real, and nobody stops for cash, records or phone calls.

questions.q: The client in the gown is going back for her handbag. What should Trudy-Ann do?
o: Go and fetch the handbag for her while she walks to the exit
Let her fetch it, as the cupboard is near the front of the salon
Tell her firmly and kindly to leave it and come out at once
Ask a stylist to fetch every client's belongings on the way out
questions.why: Nobody goes back or stops to collect belongings during an evacuation: smoke spreads faster than people expect. Belongings can be replaced; people cannot.

questions.q: Everyone is outside. How is the day's appointment list used at the assembly point?
o: To check that every client and staff member is out of the building
To phone the afternoon's clients and move their bookings to another day
To work out which services will have to be refunded or done again
To show the fire brigade which stylist was using the hood dryer
questions.why: The list shows who was in the building, so the person in charge can account for everyone and tell the fire brigade (110) at once if somebody is missing.

questions.q: A client was booked for a 45-minute pedicure at 2:30 p.m. She arrives at 2:50 p.m., and the technician's next client is booked for 3:15 p.m. How much time is left for her?
o: 25 minutes
20 minutes
30 minutes
45 minutes
questions.why: Her booked time runs from 2:30 to 3:15 p.m. She is 20 minutes late, so 45 - 20 = 25 minutes remain. The receptionist offers a shorter service or another time, so that the 3:15 p.m. client is not kept waiting.
